lesson.title: Full reading exam: evidence and paragraph functions

learning_objectives.en: Combine matching information, inference and main-idea checking in an exam-like multi-paragraph text.
learning_objectives.vi: Luyện tổng hợp ghép thông tin, suy luận và xác định ý chính của đoạn.

content.en: Spend a short moment classifying each question, then mark paragraph purpose. For inference, require more than shared vocabulary; reject unsupported absolute claims.
content.vi: Dành ít thời gian phân loại câu hỏi, sau đó nắm chức năng đoạn. Với suy luận, cần bằng chứng, tránh đáp án khẳng định tuyệt đối không được hỗ trợ.

strategies.en: Give every answer a paragraph letter and one quoted keyword of evidence. Recheck the remaining options before you commit.
strategies.vi: Mỗi đáp án cần chữ cái đoạn và từ khóa bằng chứng; loại đủ phương án trước khi chốt.

mini_review.en: For the four final MCQs, can you identify evidence rather than relying on background knowledge?
mini_review.vi: Bạn có thể chỉ ra bằng chứng cho cả bốn câu trắc nghiệm cuối?

passages.title: The radio station that kept a town informed
passages.text:
[A] When a storm cut electricity and mobile signals across the mountain town of Ridgeway for four days, most residents had no way of reading the news online. What they did have was battery radios, and a small community station run largely by volunteers became the town’s main source of information. Its two studios were in the basement of the library, which had a back-up generator.

[B] The station normally broadcasts music and local talk shows for about eight hours a day. During the emergency, it stayed on air around the clock. Volunteers read out which roads were blocked, where drinking water was available and which shops had opened. Residents who had heard the information passed it on to neighbours, so even people without radios were reached.

[C] Accuracy was a constant concern. Rumours spread quickly in the town, including a false report that the dam above the valley was about to fail. The station decided that nothing would be announced unless it had been confirmed by the emergency services or by a volunteer who had seen the situation in person. When the dam rumour was investigated and found to be untrue, the station broadcast a clear correction every hour for a day.

[D] Since the storm, the station has received funding from the regional council to install a larger generator and train more volunteers. It has also agreed a plan with the emergency services so that, in a future crisis, official announcements can be made directly from the studio. Station managers say the experience showed that new technology does not make older media unnecessary; it simply changes when they are most valuable.

[E] Listening figures have also changed. Before the storm, an estimated one in eight households tuned in at least once a week. A survey taken three months afterwards found that this had risen to one in three, and many new listeners said they had kept the habit because the station covered local events that national programmes ignored. The managers now plan a weekly programme in which residents can question council members live on air.

passages.title: How younger audiences find the news
passages.text:
[A] Ask a group of eighteen-year-olds where they last read a news story and very few will mention a newspaper. Most will name an app, a video platform or a message forwarded by a friend. This shift has worried many journalists, who fear that young people are no longer interested in the news. A three-year study of 1,200 people aged sixteen to twenty-four in the fictional country of Valdor suggests a more complicated picture: young people do follow the news, but they meet it in different ways and judge it by different standards.

[B] The most common route to the news, the study found, is accidental. Rather than deciding to read about current events, young people usually come across a story while doing something else – scrolling through photos, watching a comedy clip or chatting with friends. Around seventy per cent of participants said that most of the news they saw in a typical week had appeared in this way. Only one in five regularly visited a news website or app on purpose.

[C] This accidental exposure has advantages. It brings news to people who might never look for it, including those who say they find politics boring. However, the researchers noted that stories reached participants through systems designed to keep them watching, not to inform them. A dramatic video about a minor event could be seen by millions, while an important but less exciting decision by the government might not appear at all. Several participants admitted that they knew a great deal about celebrity disputes but very little about changes to student loans.

[D] Trust was another major theme. Participants did not trust news organisations simply because they were large or well known. Instead, they paid attention to who had shared a story and whether it seemed to be supported by evidence such as videos, documents or interviews. Many said they trusted an ordinary person filming an event more than a news presenter describing it. The researchers pointed out that this attitude can be healthy, since it encourages people to look for proof, but it also makes young audiences vulnerable to edited or misleading clips.

[E] When participants did want to understand a story properly, their habits changed. Asked what they did after seeing a surprising claim, nearly half said they searched for the same story on another source to check it. Short explainer videos and podcasts were especially popular for complicated topics such as the economy or climate policy. One participant described podcasts as “the only place where someone explains the whole story, not just the angry part”.

[F] Local news presented a particular challenge. Few participants could name a local newspaper or radio station, and many were unaware of decisions made by their town council. Yet when the researchers showed them stories about local issues – a closed youth centre, a new bus route, a plan to build flats on a sports field – interest was high. The problem, the researchers concluded, was not a lack of interest but a lack of contact: local stories rarely appear on the platforms that young people use most.

[G] Some news organisations have responded by changing how they work. In Valdor, a regional newspaper now employs two reporters who produce short videos about local stories specifically for social media, and a public broadcaster has started a weekly programme presented by people under twenty-five. Early figures suggest that these efforts reach far more young people than the organisations’ websites, although it is not yet clear whether viewers go on to read longer reports.

[H] The study’s authors argue that schools also have a role to play. Teaching students how stories are selected, how images can be edited and how to compare sources could help them make better use of the news they meet by accident. In their view, the aim should not be to persuade young people to return to traditional newspapers, but to help them become careful, questioning readers wherever they find the news.

exercises.title: Passage R-C: local radio during an emergency

instruction.en: Read the original passage and locate each kind of information in paragraphs A–E.
instruction.vi: Đọc bài gốc về radio địa phương, tìm đoạn A–E chứa thông tin.

questions.prompt_en: The initial context in which the radio service became important.
questions.prompt_vi: Bối cảnh mở đầu khiến đài phát thanh trở nên quan trọng.
questions.explanation_en: Paragraph A introduces the town and the situation.
questions.explanation_vi: Đoạn A giới thiệu bối cảnh.

questions.prompt_en: Information about what volunteers broadcast during the storm.
questions.prompt_vi: Thông tin tình nguyện viên phát trên đài trong cơn bão.
questions.explanation_en: Paragraph B lists roads, drinking water and shops.
questions.explanation_vi: Đoạn B nói đường sá, nước uống và các cửa hàng.

questions.prompt_en: A false claim that required investigation and repeated correction.
questions.prompt_vi: Tin giả phải điều tra và đính chính nhiều lần.
questions.explanation_en: Paragraph C covers the dam rumour and hourly corrections.
questions.explanation_vi: Đoạn C nói về tin đồn vỡ đập và đính chính hằng giờ.

questions.prompt_en: A later investment made after the emergency.
questions.prompt_vi: Một khoản đầu tư sau tình trạng khẩn cấp.
questions.explanation_en: Paragraph D says the station got funds to install a bigger generator.
questions.explanation_vi: Đoạn D nêu tài trợ để lắp máy phát điện lớn hơn.

questions.prompt_en: Evidence that the station gained regular listeners after the storm.
questions.prompt_vi: Bằng chứng rằng đài có thêm người nghe thường xuyên sau bão.
questions.explanation_en: Paragraph E compares one in eight households with one in three.
questions.explanation_vi: Đoạn E so sánh một phần tám hộ với một phần ba.

instruction.en: Choose ONE answer for each question based on the entire passage or general reading evidence.
instruction.vi: Chọn MỘT đáp án dựa trên toàn bài hoặc bằng chứng đọc.

questions.prompt_en: What best describes the central argument of passage R-A?
questions.prompt_vi: Luận điểm trung tâm R-A là gì?
options: Young people avoid detailed news but follow short videos.
Young people follow news through different routes and judge it differently.
Young people use social media mainly to read printed newspapers.

accepted: Young people follow news through different routes and judge it differently.

questions.explanation_en: The opening and following paragraphs describe changing access and trust patterns, not a complete rejection of news.
questions.explanation_vi: Mở bài và các đoạn sau mô tả thay đổi cách tiếp cận và độ tin, không phải tránh tin hoàn toàn.

distractors.Young people follow news through differe: Correct. The opening and following paragraphs describe changing access and trust patterns, not a complete rejection of news.
